638.title: The O Antiphons (17–23 December)
638.hook: O Wisdom, O Root of Jesse, O Key of David, O Dayspring: the verses behind O Come, O Come Emmanuel
638.howItsDone: From December 17 to 23, the Liturgy of the Hours sings one O Antiphon each evening with the Magnificat, and the same antiphons serve as the Gospel acclamation at Mass on those days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gaudete: a rose candle in the waiting, and a prisoner's word, rejoice.

A slow, slightly haunting tune turns up every December in churches, school concerts and shopping malls: O come, O come, Emmanuel. Behind its English words is something far older, sung in Latin in monastery choirs on the darkest evenings of the year: seven short chants, each beginning with the same sound, O. For many centuries, monks and nuns have sung them one a night in the last week before Christmas. A countdown, in seven names.
screen: `A FAMILIAR TUNE.` → `SEVEN OLDER CHANTS.` → `ONE A NIGHT.`

segments.voice: An antiphon is a short verse sung before and after a psalm or canticle. From December 17 to 23, at Evening Prayer, the Church sings a special one around Mary's song, the Magnificat, and each begins with O, a cry of longing. Each calls the coming Christ by a different name from the Old Testament. O Wisdom. O Adonai, the Lord who spoke to Moses in the burning bush. O Root of Jesse, from Isaiah's shoot springing from a stump. O Key of David, who opens and no one shuts. O Dayspring, the rising dawn. O King of the nations. And last, O Emmanuel, from Isaiah 7, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel." God with us. Now the hidden detail. Write down the seven Latin titles, Sapientia, Adonai, Radix, Clavis, Oriens, Rex, Emmanuel, and read their first letters backward. You get ero cras: tomorrow, I will be there. Whether a medieval monk planted that on purpose, nobody can prove. But on December 23 the last antiphon is sung, and the next night is Christmas Eve. In 1851 the Anglican priest John Mason Neale translated a Latin hymn built on these antiphons, and later revisions of his English became the carol. So when a mall speaker plays O come, O come, Emmanuel, it's carrying, faintly, the evening prayer of monasteries: seven names, each one a door Advent knocks on.

segments.voice: Choose the name that fits where you are tonight: O Wisdom, if you need to decide something; O Key, if something feels locked; O Dayspring, after a dark stretch; O Emmanuel, if you feel alone. Say it slowly with the O in front, and let the O be the whole of it, a sound of longing. If you pray, add the old ending, come; if not, just let the name sit with you.

Your line: o come. Seven names, one a night, and then Christmas Eve. Day six hundred thirty-eight, done.

639.title: Midnight Mass (Luke 2:1–14)
639.howItsDone: Catholic parishes celebrate the Mass during the Night on Christmas Eve, sometimes at midnight and often earlier, with Luke 2:1–14 as the gospel and the Gloria sung again after Advent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the O Antiphons: seven names, one a night, each a cry of longing. Your line was o come.

It's late on Christmas Eve. The presents are wrapped, or they aren't. The kids are asleep, or coming along in pajamas under their coats. And people walk into a church at an hour when nothing else is open, to hear a story that also happens at night. The church is dim, then lit. The Gloria, left out on the Sundays of Advent, comes back, and in some parishes bells ring with it. At church, Christmas begins in the dark.
screen: `LATE ON CHRISTMAS EVE.` → `A CHURCH AT AN ODD HOUR.` → `IT BEGINS IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: The Roman Missal gives Christmas four Masses: the vigil in the evening, the Mass during the night, the Mass at dawn and the Mass during the day. The night one is what people call Midnight Mass, and its gospel is Luke 2. Luke starts with an emperor. Caesar Augustus orders the whole world enrolled, and Joseph and Mary, who is with child, travel to Bethlehem because of a decree from Rome. Power at the top of the world, two people at the bottom. The birth takes one sentence. In the Douay-Rheims: "And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him up in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." A manger is a feeding trough. Then Luke turns to the night shift: shepherds in the fields, keeping the night watches over their flock. An angel appears, the glory of the Lord shines round about them, and they're terrified. Fear not, the angel says. Then a multitude of angels praises God with the line the Gloria at Mass begins with: "Glory to God in the highest; and on earth peace to men of good will." An honest note: Luke never gives the hour of the birth. Tradition ties this Mass to the night because Luke sets the shepherds there, and because an old Christmas-season chant borrows a line from the book of Wisdom: God's word leaping down from heaven while all things were in quiet silence and the night was half gone. The darkness is the point. The light shows up where people are working the night shift.

Picture the field outside Bethlehem: cold, sheep shifting, a few tired workers awake while everyone else sleeps, and then the light. If you pray, say the angels' line, glory to God in the highest; if not, let the quiet be full.

640.title: Christmas Day (John 1:1–18)
640.hook: the day Mass reads the Word made flesh
640.howItsDone: At the Mass during the Day on Christmas, Catholics hear the prologue of John's Gospel, and at the Creed the congregation kneels at the words about the incarnation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Midnight Mass: an emperor, a manger, and shepherds on the night shift. Your line was a light at midnight.

Come back to church on Christmas morning, and something odd happens. The gospel has no manger. No shepherds, no angels, no star, no donkey, no inn. Mary isn't named, and Bethlehem isn't mentioned. The reader starts before the world existed, with three words that echo the first line of Genesis: in the beginning. The night Mass told what happened in a stable. The day Mass tells who was born there.
screen: `NO MANGER, NO SHEPHERDS.` → `IN THE BEGINNING.` → `WHO WAS BORN THERE.`

segments.voice: Nativity comes from the Latin nativitas, a birth, and the Church's formal name for December 25 is the Nativity of the Lord. Its daytime gospel is the prologue of John, eighteen verses that read like a poem. In the Douay-Rheims: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." Word, in Greek, is logos: speech, reason, the meaning behind things. John says this Word made everything, and the life in him was the light of people. "And the light shineth in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it." Comprehend can mean understand, or grasp, even overpower; the Greek allows both, and translators still differ. Then the line the whole day turns on: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Flesh, not spirit dressed up as a man: skin, hunger, a body that could get cold. Dwelt literally means pitched a tent, the way God's presence lived in a tent among the Israelites in the desert. Catholics mark this line with their bodies. At the Creed each Sunday, people bow at the words about the incarnation; on Christmas and on the Annunciation, they kneel. Luke and John tell the same Christmas from two ends. Luke says: here is a baby, laid in a trough. John says: that baby is the Word that was there in the beginning. Put them together and you have the whole surprise of the day.
screen: `NATIVITAS: A BIRTH.` · `IN THE BEGINNING WAS THE WORD.` · `THE LIGHT SHINETH IN DARKNESS.` · `HE PITCHED HIS TENT AMONG US.` · then, large: `THE WORD WAS MADE FLESH.`

segments.voice: Visit a nativity scene, in a church, a store window, a neighbor's yard or on a shelf at home, or picture one you remember; Saint Francis of Assisi is said to have set up a living one at Greccio, with a real ox and donkey, so people could see how poor the birth was. Look at the smallest figure. If you pray, say John's line, the Word was made flesh; if not, just look.

641.title: Saint Stephen (26 December)
641.hook: the first martyr the day after Christmas: the crib and the cross together
641.howItsDone: Catholics keep December 26 as the feast of Saint Stephen, the first martyr, with red vestments inside the Christmas octave; in some countries it is also a day of giving to the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nativity, and John's gospel with no manger at all. Your line was the word made flesh.

December 26. The wrapping paper is in bags by the curb, there are leftovers in every container, and the tree is still lit. If you go to Mass that morning, the priest is wearing red, the color of blood. On the first day after Christmas, the Church remembers a man who was stoned to death for his faith. From lullabies to a martyrdom in a single night. The Church put it there on purpose.
screen: `THE DAY AFTER.` → `THE PRIEST WEARS RED.` → `FROM LULLABY TO MARTYR.`

segments.voice: Stephen first appears in Acts 6, in a dispute about food. The early community in Jerusalem was feeding its widows, and the Greek-speaking widows were being overlooked. So the apostles chose seven men to serve at tables, and the first named is Stephen, full of faith and of the Holy Spirit. In Catholic tradition, he was one of the first deacons. He also preached, with a power his opponents couldn't answer, and he was brought before the council. In Acts 7 he retells Israel's story, from Abraham to Moses to the temple, and it ends badly. An angry crowd drags him outside the city and stones him. As the stones fall he prays: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." Then, on his knees: "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge." Close echoes of two things Jesus says on the cross in Luke's gospel. And Luke adds a detail that matters later: the witnesses laid their cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul. Martyr comes from the Greek for witness, and Stephen's own name, stephanos, means a crown, the wreath given to a winner. Why the day after Christmas? Because the Church refuses to let the crib stay sweet. The child in the manger grows up to be crucified, and people who follow him have sometimes paid with their lives. The crib and the cross belong in the same picture. The carol Good King Wenceslas is set on this feast too: a king going out in the snow to help a poor man gathering fuel.

segments.voice: Stephen's first job was making sure widows got fed, so bring to mind someone in need you could actually help: a food bank, a neighbor short on money, a person you pass on the same corner. Then sit with his harder prayer, for the people who hurt him. If you pray, pray for someone who has wronged you; if not, simply hold them without wishing them harm.
Saint Stephen. One of the seven chosen in Jerusalem, honored by tradition as the first Christian martyr, remembered on December 26 in red. Today's word.

642.title: The Holy Innocents (28 December)
642.hook: Herod's massacre remembered; a day for all children who suffer
642.howItsDone: Catholics keep December 28 as the feast of the Holy Innocents, and many parishes and families use it to pray for children who suffer, including the unborn, refugees and children in war.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saint Stephen, in red the day after Christmas. Your line was the crib and the cross.

There's a carol from Coventry, in England, that sounds like a lullaby, soft and slow, sung by mothers to their babies. Then you listen to the words, and you realize the mothers are singing because soldiers are coming. It's from a medieval play about this day. Three days after Christmas, the Church remembers the darkest scene in the infancy story, one that nativity sets leave out. It belongs to the season anyway: Matthew tells it in the same chapter as the star.
screen: `A LULLABY FROM COVENTRY.` → `SOLDIERS ARE COMING.` → `THE SCENE THE CRIBS LEAVE OUT.`

segments.voice: In Matthew's gospel, the magi stop in Jerusalem asking where the newborn king of the Jews is. King Herod, who has a long record of killing anyone he sees as a rival, asks them to report back. They don't; they go home another way. Joseph, warned in a dream, takes Mary and the child by night and flees to Egypt. And Herod, furious, sends soldiers to kill every boy in Bethlehem and its borders two years old and under. Matthew reaches back to the prophet Jeremiah. In the Douay-Rheims: "Rachel bewailing her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not." Rachel, the wife of Jacob, was buried by tradition on the road near Bethlehem. Jeremiah pictured her weeping over her people carried into exile; Matthew hears her weeping again. An honest note: no other ancient source records this massacre. The historian Josephus describes Herod's cruelty at length, including the killing of his own sons, but not this. Bethlehem was a small village, and many scholars think the number of children would have been small too, perhaps a dozen or two, though later legends grew it into thousands. The Church honors these children as martyrs, not because they chose to die for Christ, but because they died in his place, too young to say a word. So the day has become a day for every child who suffers from the violence of the powerful: in war, in hunger, in flight, in danger at home. The Holy Family themselves end this story as refugees.
screen: `THE MAGI GO HOME ANOTHER WAY.` · `THE FLIGHT INTO EGYPT.` · `RACHEL WEEPING.` · `NO OTHER SOURCE, AND A SMALL TOWN.` · then, large: `SHE WOULD NOT BE COMFORTED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind children who are not safe tonight: in a war zone you've seen on the news, in a shelter, in a hospital, in a hard home down the street. Don't look away, and don't try to fix it in two minutes; just let them be real to you, one at a time. If you pray, pray for them by name or by place; if not, let your attention be a kind of keeping watch.

643.title: The Holy Family
643.hook: the Sunday after Christmas honors an ordinary family life
643.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of the Holy Family on the Sunday within the octave of Christmas (or on December 30 when there is no such Sunday), and some parishes bless families or renew marriage vows that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Herod, and a mother who would not be comforted. Your line was rachel weeping.

Between the infant in the manger and the grown man at the Jordan, Luke gives one scene. Jesus is twelve. The family goes up to Jerusalem for Passover with a crowd of relatives, and on the way home, a full day's walk out, Mary and Joseph realize he isn't with the cousins. Three days of searching follow. On the Sunday after Christmas, the Church sets aside the angels and the star and looks at a family: worried, tired, and very ordinary.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS OLD.` → `LOST ON THE WAY HOME.` → `THREE DAYS OF SEARCHING.`

segments.voice: They find him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening and asking questions. Mary says: your father and I have been searching for you, sorrowing. He answers that they should have known he must be about his Father's business. Luke says they didn't understand. Then the sentence the whole feast leans on. In the Douay-Rheims: "And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them." The one John called the Word that made all things goes home and does what his parents tell him. Then Luke folds every year until he is about thirty into one line: "And Jesus advanced in wisdom, and age, and grace with God and men." That's almost everything we know. Mark's gospel calls him the carpenter, using a Greek word for a builder or craftsman. The Gospels are silent about the rest: no stories of his teenage years, his friends, the day Joseph died. Tradition fills the silence with what Catholics call the hidden life, the long years at Nazareth of work, meals, prayer and village life. Today's calendar keeps the feast on the Sunday after Christmas. The point isn't that this family was perfect. Luke shows them anxious, confused, misunderstanding each other. The point is that most of the years Luke counts were spent at Nazareth, among relatives, at ordinary work. Catholics see in that a dignity for every family's daily life, the dishes included.

segments.voice: Choose one family chore you usually sigh at, the dishes, the laundry, a call to a relative you owe, and picture doing it slowly and gladly, maybe without being asked, with the faces of the people you share a life with in mind. Families come in many shapes; yours counts. If you pray, offer the chore for them; if not, simply hold them in mind.

644.title: Mary, Mother of God (1 January)
644.hook: the year begins with Mary and, since 1968, the World Day of Peace
644.howItsDone: Catholics keep January 1 as the Solemnity of Mary, the Holy Mother of God, a holy day of obligation in many countries, and the pope issues a message for the World Day of Peace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tekton: a lost boy in the temple, then long quiet years at Nazareth. Your line was an ordinary family.

Midnight on New Year's Eve: countdowns, fireworks, a phone buzzing with messages, resolutions. A few hours later, while plenty of people are still asleep, the Church holds a solemnity. The first day of the calendar year belongs to a woman: Mary, under her boldest title, Mother of God. And since 1968, it has also been the World Day of Peace. So the year opens twice: once with fireworks, and once with a mother and a prayer for peace.
screen: `MIDNIGHT, JANUARY 1.` → `THE YEAR BELONGS TO A WOMAN.` → `A DAY OF PEACE.`

segments.voice: January 1 is the octave day, the eighth day after Christmas. Luke says that on the eighth day the child was circumcised and named Jesus, and today's gospel returns to the shepherds at the manger. They tell what the angels said, everyone wonders, and Luke turns to Mary: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." While everyone else talks, she keeps and ponders. The day's title is a big one. In the year 431, bishops met at Ephesus, in what is now Turkey, to settle an argument. Nestorius, a bishop of Constantinople, had resisted calling Mary Theotokos, God-bearer, preferring Christ-bearer. The council insisted on Theotokos. It looks like an argument about Mary, but it was really about Jesus: if he is one person, truly God and truly human, then the woman who bore him bore God. Catholic and Orthodox Christians use the title; Protestant churches generally accept the council's teaching about Christ, and some use the title, while speaking about Mary in their own ways. In 1968, Pope Paul VI asked that the first day of every year be kept as a day of prayer for peace, and popes since have sent a message for it each year. The first reading is the old priestly blessing from Numbers: "The Lord bless thee, and keep thee." A mother, a blessing and peace. This week began with seven O's and ended here: o come, a light at midnight, the Word made flesh, the crib and the cross, Rachel weeping, an ordinary family, and now, begin with her.
screen: `THE EIGHTH DAY, AND A NAME.` · `MARY KEPT ALL THESE WORDS.` · `EPHESUS, 431: THEOTOKOS.` · `1968: A DAY FOR PEACE.` · then, large: `THE LORD BLESS THEE, AND KEEP THEE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one place in the world with no peace tonight, and one place in your own life: a family fight, a cold silence, a grudge. Hold both, the big and the small, without trying to solve them. If you pray, ask Mary's help or say the old blessing over that place, the Lord bless thee and keep thee; if not, simply wish peace to both.
Mary. The mother of Jesus, honored on January 1 as Mother of God, Theotokos, the one who kept all these words in her heart. Today's word.
Your line: begin with her. A new year, opened with a blessing. Happy new year, and see you tomorrow.
